sentences.text: Thaisaurus was a small ichthyopterygian, a type of marine reptile, that lived in the Early Triassic of what is now Asia.
Its skull featured enlarged, rounded eye sockets and a long, thin snout, while its mouth held narrow, pointed teeth of identical shape firmly set in extensive, partially enclosed sockets.

The animal possessed vertebrae in front of the hips that were short, contrasting with the much longer vertebrae in its tail, and it had forelimbs that were longer than its hindlimbs, both made of elongated bones.
Thaisaurus shares similarities with Chaohusaurus but also exhibits distinct anatomical differences.
The skull possessed enlarged, rounded eye sockets, suggesting a keen sense of vision.
Its vertebrae in front of the hips were short, contrasting sharply with the much longer vertebrae found in its tail.

The type specimen was discovered by Chongpan Chonglakmani on Khao Thong hill near Phattalung, Thailand, and is now housed in the Department of Mineral Resources in Bangkok with the catalog number TF2454.
Mazin and colleagues named the species Thaisaurus chonglakmanii in 1991 to honor Thailand and its discoverer, establishing the genus Thaisaurus that same year.
Maisch established the monotypic family Thaisauridae for Thaisaurus in 2010, meaning the genus is classified within this family.
Thaisaurus was an extinct marine reptile that lived during the Spathian stage of the Early Triassic, and fossils of this animal have been found in Thailand.
Motani argued in 2003 that some features considered unique to Thaisaurus were actually misinterpretations of the fossil.
